title: Trump Rolls Back Biden-Era Fuel Economy Rules, Calling Them an 'EV Mandate'
summary: President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he is rolling back fuel economy standards adopted under former President Joe Biden, arguing the change will lower car prices and boost American manufacturing. In a social media post, Trump said the new standards would "TERMINATE" what he called Biden's "EV mandate" — though there is no federal law requiring Americans to buy electric vehicles. At the center of the debate are Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, established by Congress in 1975. These rules require automakers to meet average fuel economy targets across all cars and light trucks they sell. Under Biden-era rules finalized in 2024, the required fleetwide average was set to rise from 39.1 miles per gallon (mpg) to about 50.4 mpg by 2031. The Biden administration said the rules would cut fuel consumption and emissions to fight climate change while saving drivers money at the pump. Trump did not provide exact numbers for his new standards, but in December 2025 he proposed a fleetwide average of roughly 34.5 mpg by 2031 — more than 30 percent lower than Biden's rule. "These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car," Trump wrote. The Republican-controlled Congress already gutted consumer tax incentives for electric vehicles last year as part of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an announcement would be "COMING MONDAY." Supporters say the rollback helps carmakers and buyers. Critics argue it will increase pollution and widen the gap between U.S. policy and global trends favoring electric vehicles.
why_it_matters: Fuel economy rules decide what kinds of cars get built for the next decade, which shapes how much pollution the U.S. produces, how much families pay for fuel and whether American automakers stay competitive with the fast-growing electric-vehicle industries in China and Europe. Because the standards swing with each administration, today's teenagers will likely see several reversals before they buy their own first car.

background_read: CAFE standards are older than most people assume: Congress created them in 1975, just after the 1973 oil crisis, when an oil embargo sent gasoline prices soaring and the U.S. wanted to depend less on imported oil.

Since then, how strict those rules are has swung back and forth depending on which party holds the White House — tighter under Democratic administrations, looser under Republican ones — so automakers plan years ahead while knowing the targets may change.

Joe Biden (U.S. president from 2021 to 2025) argued tougher standards would cut pollution and save drivers money at the pump; Donald Trump (president again since 2025) argues they raise car prices and cost American manufacturing jobs.

Because CAFE sets an average rather than a cap on any single model, automakers can still sell big pickups and SUVs as long as they also sell enough efficient vehicles — which is why the rule shapes the mix of cars on dealer lots rather than banning any type of vehicle.

Transportation is the largest single source of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, so fuel economy rules are one of the country's main climate tools, sitting alongside international efforts such as the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Sean Duffy (the U.S. transportation secretary) said details were 'COMING MONDAY,' and automakers, states and environmental groups are all watching because the final numbers are likely to end up in court.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — cheaper cars and a boost for U.S. manufacturing
perspectives.description: Trump and supporters argue that less demanding mileage targets cut the cost of building cars, and those savings get passed to families buying new vehicles. They also say the Biden rules pushed technology faster than charging networks and buyers were ready for, and that loosening them keeps factories and jobs in the United States.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — more pollution, less global competitiveness
perspectives.description: Critics say weaker standards mean more gasoline burned and more greenhouse gases released, at a time when transportation is already the biggest source of U.S. emissions. They warn that slowing EV adoption widens the gap between American automakers and rivals in China and Europe, who are investing heavily in electric models.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — a rule that has always swung
perspectives.description: CAFE standards have been tightened under Democratic presidents and relaxed under Republican ones since the 1970s, so automakers design vehicles knowing the targets may shift again. Because the standard is a fleetwide average, it doesn't ban any model — it just changes the balance of efficient cars and large trucks a company needs to sell.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — the fight moves to the details and the courts
perspectives.description: The exact numbers are expected soon, and the December 2025 proposal of roughly 34.5 mpg by 2031 is already on record. Legal challenges from states and environmental groups are likely, the 2028 election could reverse the policy again, and the long-term question is whether the U.S. keeps pace with a global auto industry that is steadily electrifying.
